al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom, saying: give thanks to Me."

It is also said: "that give thanks to Me," so he gave thanks, and so he was wise through his thankfulness. Thanks to Allah is praise of Him in return for a blessing and obedience to what He has commanded.

Then Allah – glorified be He – made clear that thanks benefits no one but the one who gives thanks, so He said: ﴿ومَن يَشْكُرْ فَإنَّما يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ﴾ ("Whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own self"), because the benefit of that returns to him, and its fruit accrues to him, for by it blessings are preserved and by its means more of them are drawn from Allah – glorified be He. (p-1142) ﴿ومَن كَفَرَ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ غَنِيٌّ حَمِيدٌ﴾ ("And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy"), meaning: whoever makes the denial of blessings in place of thanking for them – Allah is Free of need from his thanks, not in need of it, Praiseworthy, deserving of praise from His creation for His favours upon them, blessings whose measure cannot be encompassed and whose number cannot be counted, even if none of His creatures praises Him, for every existing thing is speaking His praise with the tongue of its state.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: "Free of need from His creation, Praiseworthy in His acts."

﴿وإذْ قالَ لُقْمانُ لِابْنِهِ﴾ ("And when Luqman said to his son"). al-Suhayli said: the name of his son is Tharan according to Ibn Jarir and al-Qutaybi. al-Kalbi said: Mishkam. al-Naqqash said: Anʿam. It was said: Matan. al-Qushayri said: his son and his wife were disbelievers, and he never ceased admonishing them until they both embraced Islam. This sentence is coordinated with what preceded, and the implied sense is: "We gave Luqman wisdom when We made him grateful in himself, and when We made him an admonisher to others."

al-Zajjaj said: *idh* is in the accusative position governed by *ataynā*, and the meaning is: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom when he said..."

al-Nahhas said: I think this is an error, because there is a waw in the sentence and it prevents that.

The meaning of ﴿وهُوَ يَعِظُهُ﴾ ("while he was admonishing him") is that he addressed him with admonitions that encourage him toward monotheism and turn him away from polytheism. ﴿يابُنَيَّ لا تُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ﴾ ("O my son, do not associate anything with Allah"). The majority read *yā-bunayya* with a kasra on the ya. Ibn Kathir read it with sukun. Hafs read it with fatha. His prohibition of polytheism shows that he was a disbeliever, as mentioned earlier. The sentence ﴿إنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong") is a reason for what precedes. He began his admonition with forbidding polytheism because it is more important than anything else.

There is a difference about this sentence: it is said to be part of Luqman's speech, and it is said to be part of Allah's speech, in which case it is disconnected from what precedes. This is supported by the authentic hadith that when ﴿ولَمْ يَلْبِسُوا إيمانَهم بِظُلْمٍ﴾ ("and they have not mixed their belief with wrongdoing") [al-Anʿam: 82] was revealed, it was hard on the Companions, and they said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" So Allah revealed ﴿إنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾, and their hearts were content.

﴿ووَصَّيْنا الإنْسانَ بِوالِدَيْهِ﴾ ("And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents"). This injunction concerning the parents, and what follows up to His words ﴿بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("of what you used to do"), is an interjection between Luqman's speech, intended to emphasise what preceded of the prohibition of associating anything with Allah. The explanation of the injunction is His words ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي ولِوالِدَيْكَ﴾ ("give thanks to Me and to your parents"), and what lies between them is an interjection between the explanation and the thing explained. Joining thanks to them with thanks to Allah indicates that their right is among the greatest rights upon the child, the greatest and the most binding. The meaning of ﴿حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ وهْنًا عَلى وهْنٍ﴾ ("his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness") is that she carried him in her womb while growing weaker each day upon weakness. It was also said: the meaning is that a woman is weak by nature, and then pregnancy weakens her further. *Wahnan* is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar).

al-Nahhas said: it is in the accusative as a second object, with the preposition removed, i.e., she carried him with weakness upon weakness. al-Zajjaj said the meaning is that carrying him necessitated that she weaken time after time. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of *ummuhu*, and ﴿عَلى وهْنٍ﴾ ("upon weakness") is a description of *wahnan*, i.e., a weakness existing upon weakness. The majority read the *hā'* with sukun in both places.

ʿĪsā al-Thaqafi – and it is a transmission from Abu ʿAmr – read it with fatha in both places, and both are dialectal forms. Qa'nab said:

*Is there for the blamers any forbidder who will restrain them? Indeed, in them are exhaustion and weakness.*

﴿وفِصالُهُ في عامَيْنِ﴾ ("and his weaning is in two years"). *al-Fisal* is weaning, which is that the child is separated from the mother. It is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the adverbial phrase.

al-Jahdari, Qatada, Abu Raja', al-Hasan and Ya'qub read *wa-faṣluhu*, and both are dialectal forms. It is said: *infaṣala ʿan kadhā*, meaning separated/distinguished from such-and-such, and from this the young camel (faṣīl) is named.

We have already mentioned that *an* in ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي ولِوالِدَيْكَ﴾ is explanatory.

al-Zajjaj said: it is verbal-infinitival (maṣdariyya), meaning: "by [saying] give thanks to Me." al-Nahhas said: what is better than this is that *an* is explanatory. The sentence ﴿إلَيَّ المَصِيرُ﴾ ("to Me is the destination") is a reason for the obligation to comply with the command, i.e., returning to Me, not to another.

﴿وإنْ جاهَداكَ عَلى أنْ تُشْرِكَ بِي ما لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ ("And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge"), meaning: that whose partnership you have no knowledge of, ﴿فَلا تُطِعْهُما﴾ ("then do not obey them") in that.

We have already mentioned the explanation of this verse and its occasion of revelation in Surat al-ʿAnkabut. The accusative of ﴿مَعْرُوفًا﴾ ("kindly") is as a description of an omitted infinitive, i.e., "accompany them in a kind companionship." It was also said: it is accusative by removal of the preposition, the implied sense being "with kindness."

﴿واتَّبِعْ سَبِيلَ مَن أنابَ إلَيَّ﴾ ("and follow the way of those who turn to Me"), i.e., follow the way of those of My righteous servants who have returned to Me in repentance and sincerity. ﴿ثُمَّ إلَيَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ﴾ ("then to Me is your return") all of you, not to another. ﴿فَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ﴾ ("then I will inform you") – i.e., I will tell you when you return – ﴿بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("of what you used to do") of good and evil, and I will recompense every doer for his deed.

It has been said that this context, from His words ﴿ووَصَّيْنا الإنْسانَ﴾ up to here, is part of Luqman's speech, and so it is not an interjection; but this is far-fetched.

Then Allah – glorified be He – began relating the remainder of Luqman's speech in his admonition to his son, saying: ﴿يابُنَيَّ إنَّها إنْ تَكُ مِثْقالَ حَبَّةٍ مِن خَرْدَلٍ﴾ ("O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed"). The pronoun in *innahā* refers to the wrongdoing (khaṭī'a), because it is reported that Luqman's son said to his father: "O father, if I commit a wrong where no one sees me, does Allah know it?" So he said: "Indeed it" – i.e., the wrong – and the conditional clause explains the pronoun, i.e., indeed the wrong, if it be the weight of a mustard seed.

al-Zajjaj said: the implied sense is: "Indeed that which you asked me about, if it be the weight of a mustard seed." He expressed it by the mustard seed because it is the smallest of seeds, whose weight is not perceived by the senses and does not tip a scale.

It was also said: the pronoun in "innahā" refers to the kind of deed of evil and good, i.e., indeed the kind of evil and good deed, if it be the weight of a mustard seed, etc. Then he increased the explanation of the seed's concealment together with its lightness, saying: ﴿فَتَكُنْ في صَخْرَةٍ﴾ ("then it will be in a rock"), for its being in a rock is in the most hidden and most secure place. ﴿أوْ في السَّماواتِ أوْ في الأرْضِ﴾ ("or in the heavens or in the earth"), i.e., or wherever it may be among the places of the heavens or the places of the earth. ﴿يَأْتِ بِها اللَّهُ﴾ ("Allah will bring it forth"), i.e., He will produce it and call its doer to account for it. ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لَطِيفٌ﴾ ("Indeed Allah is Subtle") – nothing hidden is concealed from Him, rather His knowledge reaches every hidden thing – ﴿خَبِيرٌ﴾ ("Aware") of everything; nothing escapes Him.

The majority read *in takun* with the feminine ta', meaning: "if the wrong, or the matter, or the deed, or the story be..." They read *mithqāla* with the accusative as the predicate of *kāna*, its subject being one of those implied things. Nafi' read *mithqālu* with nominative as the subject of *kāna*, which is complete (tāmma). He made the verb feminine in this reading because *mithqāl* is annexed to a feminine noun.

The majority read *fa-takun* with a damma on the kaf. al-Jahdari read it with a kasra and a shadda on the nun, from *kanna*, which is that which is covered.

al-Suddi said: this rock is a rock which is neither in the heavens nor in the earth.

Then Allah – glorified be He – related of Luqman that he commanded his son to establish the prayer, to enjoin what is good, to forbid what is evil, and to be patient over calamity.

The reason for singling out these acts of obedience is that they are the mothers of acts of worship and the pillar of all good.

The reference in ﴿إنَّ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("Indeed that") is to the aforementioned acts of obedience. The predicate of *inna* is His words ﴿مِن عَزْمِ الأُمُورِ﴾ ("among the matters requiring determination"), i.e., among what Allah has made a firm resolve and obligated upon His servants. It was also said: the meaning is "from the due of matters which Allah has commanded." *ʿAzm* may be taken in the sense of the object determined (maʿzūm), i.e., of determined matters, or in the sense of the one determining (ʿāzim), as in His words ﴿فَإذا عَزَمَ الأمْرُ﴾ ("then when the matter is determined") [Muhammad: 21]. al-Mubarrad said: the ʿayn is changed to ḥā', so it is said *ʿazm* and *ḥazm*.

Ibn Jarir said: it may be meant that this is among the noble qualities of people of character and the firm resolutions of people of prudence who travel the path of salvation. al-Qurtubi endorsed this.

"And do not turn your cheek away from people" (*wa-lā tuṣāʿir khaddaka lil-nās*). The majority read *tuṣaʿʿir* (with shadda), while Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and ʿĀsim read *tuṣāʿir*, and the meaning is close. *Ṣaʿar* is inclination: one says *ṣaʿʿara khaddahu* and *ṣāʿara khaddahu* when he inclines his face and turns away out of arrogance. The meaning: do not turn away from people in pride over them. From this is the poet's saying:

*And when the tyrant turned his cheek away, we would walk to him with swords, rebuking him.*

Ibn Jarir narrated it thus:

*And when the tyrant turned his cheek away, we would set him straight from his inclination, and he would straighten.*

al-Harawi said: "Do not turn your cheek away from people" means: do not turn away from them in arrogance. One says: the camel was afflicted with *ṣaʿar*, when he was struck by a disease that twists his neck. It was also said: the meaning is: do not twist your jaw when a man is mentioned in your presence, as if you despise him.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: it seems He forbade a person from humbling himself without need, and perhaps he understood from *taṣʿīr* the meaning of abasement.

"And do not walk upon the earth exultantly" (*wa-lā tamshi fil-arḍi maraḥan*), i.e., in self-admiration and joy. The meaning is the prohibition of arrogance and haughtiness. The one who is self-admiring (*mukhtāl*) struts in his walk. It is an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, and its verification has already been mentioned. His words ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخْتالٍ فَخُورٍ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-admiring and boastful") are a reason for the prohibition, because *ikhtiyāl* is *maraḥ*, and the *fakhūr* is one who boasts over people with his wealth, nobility, strength, or other things. Speaking of Allah's blessings is not included in this, for Allah says: ﴿وأمّا بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ فَحَدِّثْ﴾ ("And as for the favour of your Lord, speak of it") [al-Duha: 11].

"And be moderate in your walking" (*wa-iqṣid fī mashyika*), i.e., be balanced in it. *Qaṣd* is between hastening and slowness. One says: so-and-so *qaṣada* in his gait when he walks evenly, neither creeping like the feigned-sick, nor leaping like the devils.

It is established that the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – "when he walked, he hastened." So the *qaṣd* here must be understood as what exceeds the limit in speed. Muqatil said: its meaning is: do not stumble in your walk. ʿAṭāʾ said: walk with dignity and tranquility, like His words ﴿يَمْشُونَ عَلى الأرْضِ هَوْنًا﴾ ("who walk upon the earth in humility") [al-Furqan: 63].

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah 31, verses 12–19 (part 2 of 2):

﴿وَاغْضُضْ مِن صَوْتِكَ﴾ means: reduce it and lower it, and do not force yourself to raise it, for raising the voice more than is needed harms the listener. The clause ﴿إِنَّ أَنكَرَ الأَصْوَاتِ لَصَوْتُ الْحَمِيرِ﴾ gives the reason for the command to lower the voice, meaning: the most repellent and ugliest of voices. Qatadah said: "The ugliest of voices is the voice of donkeys; its beginning is a groan (zafir) and its end is a sob (shahiq)." Al-Mubarrad said: "Its interpretation is that raising the voice is not praiseworthy, and that it falls under the category of objectionable sounds." The lam in ﴿لَصَوْتُ﴾ is for emphasis. The word "voice" (ṣawt) is in the singular even though it is attached to a plural, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and a maṣdar indicates multiplicity. It is the maṣdar of ṣāta, yaṣūtu, ṣawtan, so the one who does it is ṣā'it.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what Luqman was?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "He was an Abyssinian."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-Mamlukin*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban in *al-Du'afa'*, and Ibn Asakir reported from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Take the Sudanese (as servants), for three of them are masters of the people of Paradise: Luqman the wise, al-Najjashi (the Negus), and Bilal the muezzin." Al-Tabarani said: He meant the Abyssinians.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, concerning God's words ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا لُقْمَانَ الْحِكْمَةَ﴾ (And We indeed gave Luqman wisdom), that it means intellect, understanding and sagacity, without prophethood.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ikrimah that he was a prophet. We have already mentioned that the one who narrates from him is Jabir al-Ju'fi, who is extremely weak.

Ahmad, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim in *al-Kuna*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Luqman the wise used to say: Indeed, when God is entrusted with something, He preserves it."

A group of the people of hadith have transmitted reports from a number of Companions and Successors containing sayings from Luqman's admonitions and maxims. Nothing from them has been authentically established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), nor has any sound chain of transmission been established back to Luqman for any of them, so that we could accept it. God, glorified is He, has related from his admonitions to his son what He has related in this passage, and that is sufficient. Anything beyond that which is not authentic has no purpose in being mentioned except to waste space and occupy time. Nor was he a prophet, such that what is reported from him would be the law of earlier communities (shar' man qablana, the revealed law of those before us). Nor is there a sound chain for the words reported from him, such that recording them would be a compilation of the words of wisdom, which are the "lost property of the believer."

Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir reported from Abu Uthman al-Nahdi that Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: This verse was revealed concerning me: ﴿وَإِنْ جَاهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰ أَن تُشْرِكَ بِي﴾ (And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me...). This has already been mentioned.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: This verse was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ﴾ (weakness upon weakness), that he said: hardship after hardship and creation after creation.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Adi and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about God's words ﴿وَلَا تُصَعِّرْ خَدَّكَ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ (And do not turn your cheek away from people in contempt), and he said: "Twisting of the cheek (liyy al-shidq)." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning the same verse, that it means: do not be arrogant, so that you despise God's servants and turn away from them when they speak to you.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning the verse that it refers to the one who, when greeted, twists his neck like one who is arrogant.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 31, verse 12–19 (part 1 of 2):

There is a difference of opinion about Luqman: is he a non-Arab (ʿajamī) or an Arab? He is said to be derived from al-luqam (mouthfuls). Whoever says he is a non-Arab prohibits his name from taking tanwin because of its being a proper name (ta'rif) and foreignness (ʿujma), and whoever says he is an Arab prohibits it from taking tanwin because of its being a proper name and the added alif and nun.

They also differed over whether he was a prophet (nabi) or a righteous man (rajul ṣāliḥ). The majority of scholars hold that he was not a prophet.

al-Wahidi transmitted from ʿIkrima, al-Suddi and al-Shaʿbi that he was a prophet, but the first view is more likely, for reasons that will come at the end of this discussion.

It is said that only ʿIkrima affirmed his prophethood, and the narrator of this from him is Jabir al-Ju'fi, who is extremely weak. He was Luqman ibn Baʿura ibn Nahur ibn Tarikh, and he was Azar, the father of Ibrahim. It is also said that he was Luqman ibn ʿAnqa ibn Marwan, a Nubian from the people of Ayla, mentioned by al-Suhayli.

Wahb said: he was the son of Ayyub's sister.

Muqatil said: he was the son of Ayyub's maternal aunt. He lived a thousand years, took knowledge from him, and used to give legal rulings (yufti) before the mission of Dawud. When Dawud was sent, he ceased giving rulings. It was said to him, "Why?" He said, "Shall I not be content, since I have been relieved of it?"

al-Waqidi said: he was a judge among the Children of Israel. The wisdom (hikma) that Allah gave him is understanding (fiqh), intellect, and correctness in speech. Whoever holds that he was a prophet explains the wisdom as prophethood. In ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي﴾ ("that give thanks to Me"), the *an* is explanatory (mufassira), because the granting of wisdom carries the meaning of saying.

It is also said that the implied sense is: "We said to him, give thanks to Me."

al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom, saying: give thanks to Me."

It is also said: "that give thanks to Me," so he gave thanks, and so he was wise through his thankfulness. Thanks to Allah is praise of Him in return for a blessing and obedience to what He has commanded.

Then Allah – glorified be He – made clear that thanks benefits no one but the one who gives thanks, so He said: ﴿ومَن يَشْكُرْ فَإنَّما يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ﴾ ("Whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own self"), because the benefit of that returns to him, and its fruit accrues to him, for by it blessings are preserved and by its means more of them are drawn from Allah – glorified be He. (p-1142) ﴿ومَن كَفَرَ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ غَنِيٌّ حَمِيدٌ﴾ ("And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy"), meaning: whoever makes the denial of blessings in place of thanking for them – Allah is Free of need from his thanks, not in need of it, Praiseworthy, deserving of praise from His creation for His favours upon them, blessings whose measure cannot be encompassed and whose number cannot be counted, even if none of His creatures praises Him, for every existing thing is speaking His praise with the tongue of its state.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: "Free of need from His creation, Praiseworthy in His acts."

﴿وإذْ قالَ لُقْمانُ لِابْنِهِ﴾ ("And when Luqman said to his son"). al-Suhayli said: the name of his son is Tharan according to Ibn Jarir and al-Qutaybi. al-Kalbi said: Mishkam. al-Naqqash said: Anʿam. It was said: Matan. al-Qushayri said: his son and his wife were disbelievers, and he never ceased admonishing them until they both embraced Islam. This sentence is coordinated with what preceded, and the implied sense is: "We gave Luqman wisdom when We made him grateful in himself, and when We made him an admonisher to others."

al-Zajjaj said: *idh* is in the accusative position governed by *ataynā*, and the meaning is: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom when he said..."

al-Nahhas said: I think this is an error, because there is a waw in the sentence and it prevents that.

The meaning of ﴿وهُوَ يَعِظُهُ﴾ ("while he was admonishing him") is that he addressed him with admonitions that encourage him toward monotheism and turn him away from polytheism. ﴿يابُنَيَّ لا تُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ﴾ ("O my son, do not associate anything with Allah"). The majority read *yā-bunayya* with a kasra on the ya. Ibn Kathir read it with sukun. Hafs read it with fatha. His prohibition of polytheism shows that he was a disbeliever, as mentioned earlier. The sentence ﴿إنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong") is a reason for what precedes. He began his admonition with forbidding polytheism because it is more important than anything else.

There is a difference about this sentence: it is said to be part of Luqman's speech, and it is said to be part of Allah's speech, in which case it is disconnected from what precedes. This is supported by the authentic hadith that when ﴿ولَمْ يَلْبِسُوا إيمانَهم بِظُلْمٍ﴾ ("and they have not mixed their belief with wrongdoing") [al-Anʿam: 82] was revealed, it was hard on the Companions, and they said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" So Allah revealed ﴿إنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾, and their hearts were content.

﴿ووَصَّيْنا الإنْسانَ بِوالِدَيْهِ﴾ ("And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents"). This injunction concerning the parents, and what follows up to His words ﴿بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("of what you used to do"), is an interjection between Luqman's speech, intended to emphasise what preceded of the prohibition of associating anything with Allah. The explanation of the injunction is His words ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي ولِوالِدَيْكَ﴾ ("give thanks to Me and to your parents"), and what lies between them is an interjection between the explanation and the thing explained. Joining thanks to them with thanks to Allah indicates that their right is among the greatest rights upon the child, the greatest and the most binding. The meaning of ﴿حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ وهْنًا عَلى وهْنٍ﴾ ("his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness") is that she carried him in her womb while growing weaker each day upon weakness. It was also said: the meaning is that a woman is weak by nature, and then pregnancy weakens her further. *Wahnan* is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar).

al-Nahhas said: it is in the accusative as a second object, with the preposition removed, i.e., she carried him with weakness upon weakness. al-Zajjaj said the meaning is that carrying him necessitated that she weaken time after time. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of *ummuhu*, and ﴿عَلى وهْنٍ﴾ ("upon weakness") is a description of *wahnan*, i.e., a weakness existing upon weakness. The majority read the *hā'* with sukun in both places.

ʿĪsā al-Thaqafi – and it is a transmission from Abu ʿAmr – read it with fatha in both places, and both are dialectal forms. Qa'nab said:

*Is there for the blamers any forbidder who will restrain them? Indeed, in them are exhaustion and weakness.*

﴿وفِصالُهُ في عامَيْنِ﴾ ("and his weaning is in two years"). *al-Fisal* is weaning, which is that the child is separated from the mother. It is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the adverbial phrase.

al-Jahdari, Qatada, Abu Raja', al-Hasan and Ya'qub read *wa-faṣluhu*, and both are dialectal forms. It is said: *infaṣala ʿan kadhā*, meaning separated/distinguished from such-and-such, and from this the young camel (faṣīl) is named.

We have already mentioned that *an* in ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي ولِوالِدَيْكَ﴾ is explanatory.

al-Zajjaj said: it is verbal-infinitival (maṣdariyya), meaning: "by [saying] give thanks to Me." al-Nahhas said: what is better than this is that *an* is explanatory. The sentence ﴿إلَيَّ المَصِيرُ﴾ ("to Me is the destination") is a reason for the obligation to comply with the command, i.e., returning to Me, not to another.

﴿وإنْ جاهَداكَ عَلى أنْ تُشْرِكَ بِي ما لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ ("And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge"), meaning: that whose partnership you have no knowledge of, ﴿فَلا تُطِعْهُما﴾ ("then do not obey them") in that.

We have already mentioned the explanation of this verse and its occasion of revelation in Surat al-ʿAnkabut. The accusative of ﴿مَعْرُوفًا﴾ ("kindly") is as a description of an omitted infinitive, i.e., "accompany them in a kind companionship." It was also said: it is accusative by removal of the preposition, the implied sense being "with kindness."

﴿واتَّبِعْ سَبِيلَ مَن أنابَ إلَيَّ﴾ ("and follow the way of those who turn to Me"), i.e., follow the way of those of My righteous servants who have returned to Me in repentance and sincerity. ﴿ثُمَّ إلَيَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ﴾ ("then to Me is your return") all of you, not to another. ﴿فَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ﴾ ("then I will inform you") – i.e., I will tell you when you return – ﴿بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("of what you used to do") of good and evil, and I will recompense every doer for his deed.

It has been said that this context, from His words ﴿ووَصَّيْنا الإنْسانَ﴾ up to here, is part of Luqman's speech, and so it is not an interjection; but this is far-fetched.

Then Allah – glorified be He – began relating the remainder of Luqman's speech in his admonition to his son, saying: ﴿يابُنَيَّ إنَّها إنْ تَكُ مِثْقالَ حَبَّةٍ مِن خَرْدَلٍ﴾ ("O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed"). The pronoun in *innahā* refers to the wrongdoing (khaṭī'a), because it is reported that Luqman's son said to his father: "O father, if I commit a wrong where no one sees me, does Allah know it?" So he said: "Indeed it" – i.e., the wrong – and the conditional clause explains the pronoun, i.e., indeed the wrong, if it be the weight of a mustard seed.

al-Zajjaj said: the implied sense is: "Indeed that which you asked me about, if it be the weight of a mustard seed." He expressed it by the mustard seed because it is the smallest of seeds, whose weight is not perceived by the senses and does not tip a scale.

It was also said: the pronoun in "innahā" refers to the kind of deed of evil and good, i.e., indeed the kind of evil and good deed, if it be the weight of a mustard seed, etc. Then he increased the explanation of the seed's concealment together with its lightness, saying: ﴿فَتَكُنْ في صَخْرَةٍ﴾ ("then it will be in a rock"), for its being in a rock is in the most hidden and most secure place. ﴿أوْ في السَّماواتِ أوْ في الأرْضِ﴾ ("or in the heavens or in the earth"), i.e., or wherever it may be among the places of the heavens or the places of the earth. ﴿يَأْتِ بِها اللَّهُ﴾ ("Allah will bring it forth"), i.e., He will produce it and call its doer to account for it. ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لَطِيفٌ﴾ ("Indeed Allah is Subtle") – nothing hidden is concealed from Him, rather His knowledge reaches every hidden thing – ﴿خَبِيرٌ﴾ ("Aware") of everything; nothing escapes Him.

The majority read *in takun* with the feminine ta', meaning: "if the wrong, or the matter, or the deed, or the story be..." They read *mithqāla* with the accusative as the predicate of *kāna*, its subject being one of those implied things. Nafi' read *mithqālu* with nominative as the subject of *kāna*, which is complete (tāmma). He made the verb feminine in this reading because *mithqāl* is annexed to a feminine noun.

The majority read *fa-takun* with a damma on the kaf. al-Jahdari read it with a kasra and a shadda on the nun, from *kanna*, which is that which is covered.

al-Suddi said: this rock is a rock which is neither in the heavens nor in the earth.

Then Allah – glorified be He – related of Luqman that he commanded his son to establish the prayer, to enjoin what is good, to forbid what is evil, and to be patient over calamity.

The reason for singling out these acts of obedience is that they are the mothers of acts of worship and the pillar of all good.

The reference in ﴿إنَّ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("Indeed that") is to the aforementioned acts of obedience. The predicate of *inna* is His words ﴿مِن عَزْمِ الأُمُورِ﴾ ("among the matters requiring determination"), i.e., among what Allah has made a firm resolve and obligated upon His servants. It was also said: the meaning is "from the due of matters which Allah has commanded." *ʿAzm* may be taken in the sense of the object determined (maʿzūm), i.e., of determined matters, or in the sense of the one determining (ʿāzim), as in His words ﴿فَإذا عَزَمَ الأمْرُ﴾ ("then when the matter is determined") [Muhammad: 21]. al-Mubarrad said: the ʿayn is changed to ḥā', so it is said *ʿazm* and *ḥazm*.

Ibn Jarir said: it may be meant that this is among the noble qualities of people of character and the firm resolutions of people of prudence who travel the path of salvation. al-Qurtubi endorsed this.

"And do not turn your cheek away from people" (*wa-lā tuṣāʿir khaddaka lil-nās*). The majority read *tuṣaʿʿir* (with shadda), while Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and ʿĀsim read *tuṣāʿir*, and the meaning is close. *Ṣaʿar* is inclination: one says *ṣaʿʿara khaddahu* and *ṣāʿara khaddahu* when he inclines his face and turns away out of arrogance. The meaning: do not turn away from people in pride over them. From this is the poet's saying:

*And when the tyrant turned his cheek away, we would walk to him with swords, rebuking him.*

Ibn Jarir narrated it thus:

*And when the tyrant turned his cheek away, we would set him straight from his inclination, and he would straighten.*

al-Harawi said: "Do not turn your cheek away from people" means: do not turn away from them in arrogance. One says: the camel was afflicted with *ṣaʿar*, when he was struck by a disease that twists his neck. It was also said: the meaning is: do not twist your jaw when a man is mentioned in your presence, as if you despise him.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: it seems He forbade a person from humbling himself without need, and perhaps he understood from *taṣʿīr* the meaning of abasement.

"And do not walk upon the earth exultantly" (*wa-lā tamshi fil-arḍi maraḥan*), i.e., in self-admiration and joy. The meaning is the prohibition of arrogance and haughtiness. The one who is self-admiring (*mukhtāl*) struts in his walk. It is an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, and its verification has already been mentioned. His words ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخْتالٍ فَخُورٍ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-admiring and boastful") are a reason for the prohibition, because *ikhtiyāl* is *maraḥ*, and the *fakhūr* is one who boasts over people with his wealth, nobility, strength, or other things. Speaking of Allah's blessings is not included in this, for Allah says: ﴿وأمّا بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ فَحَدِّثْ﴾ ("And as for the favour of your Lord, speak of it") [al-Duha: 11].

"And be moderate in your walking" (*wa-iqṣid fī mashyika*), i.e., be balanced in it. *Qaṣd* is between hastening and slowness. One says: so-and-so *qaṣada* in his gait when he walks evenly, neither creeping like the feigned-sick, nor leaping like the devils.

It is established that the Messenger of Allah – may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace – "when he walked, he hastened." So the *qaṣd* here must be understood as what exceeds the limit in speed. Muqatil said: its meaning is: do not stumble in your walk. ʿAṭāʾ said: walk with dignity and tranquility, like His words ﴿يَمْشُونَ عَلى الأرْضِ هَوْنًا﴾ ("who walk upon the earth in humility") [al-Furqan: 63].

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah 31, verses 12–19 (part 2 of 2):

﴿وَاغْضُضْ مِن صَوْتِكَ﴾ means: reduce it and lower it, and do not force yourself to raise it, for raising the voice more than is needed harms the listener. The clause ﴿إِنَّ أَنكَرَ الأَصْوَاتِ لَصَوْتُ الْحَمِيرِ﴾ gives the reason for the command to lower the voice, meaning: the most repellent and ugliest of voices. Qatadah said: "The ugliest of voices is the voice of donkeys; its beginning is a groan (zafir) and its end is a sob (shahiq)." Al-Mubarrad said: "Its interpretation is that raising the voice is not praiseworthy, and that it falls under the category of objectionable sounds." The lam in ﴿لَصَوْتُ﴾ is for emphasis. The word "voice" (ṣawt) is in the singular even though it is attached to a plural, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and a maṣdar indicates multiplicity. It is the maṣdar of ṣāta, yaṣūtu, ṣawtan, so the one who does it is ṣā'it.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what Luqman was?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "He was an Abyssinian."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-Mamlukin*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban in *al-Du'afa'*, and Ibn Asakir reported from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Take the Sudanese (as servants), for three of them are masters of the people of Paradise: Luqman the wise, al-Najjashi (the Negus), and Bilal the muezzin." Al-Tabarani said: He meant the Abyssinians.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported from him, concerning God's words ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا لُقْمَانَ الْحِكْمَةَ﴾ (And We indeed gave Luqman wisdom), that it means intellect, understanding and sagacity, without prophethood.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ikrimah that he was a prophet. We have already mentioned that the one who narrates from him is Jabir al-Ju'fi, who is extremely weak.

Ahmad, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim in *al-Kuna*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Luqman the wise used to say: Indeed, when God is entrusted with something, He preserves it."

A group of the people of hadith have transmitted reports from a number of Companions and Successors containing sayings from Luqman's admonitions and maxims. Nothing from them has been authentically established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), nor has any sound chain of transmission been established back to Luqman for any of them, so that we could accept it. God, glorified is He, has related from his admonitions to his son what He has related in this passage, and that is sufficient. Anything beyond that which is not authentic has no purpose in being mentioned except to waste space and occupy time. Nor was he a prophet, such that what is reported from him would be the law of earlier communities (shar' man qablana, the revealed law of those before us). Nor is there a sound chain for the words reported from him, such that recording them would be a compilation of the words of wisdom, which are the "lost property of the believer."

Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir reported from Abu Uthman al-Nahdi that Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: This verse was revealed concerning me: ﴿وَإِنْ جَاهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰ أَن تُشْرِكَ بِي﴾ (And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me...). This has already been mentioned.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu Hurayrah that he said: This verse was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ﴾ (weakness upon weakness), that he said: hardship after hardship and creation after creation.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Adi and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about God's words ﴿وَلَا تُصَعِّرْ خَدَّكَ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ (And do not turn your cheek away from people in contempt), and he said: "Twisting of the cheek (liyy al-shidq)." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning the same verse, that it means: do not be arrogant, so that you despise God's servants and turn away from them when they speak to you.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning the verse that it refers to the one who, when greeted, twists his neck like one who is arrogant.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 31, verse 12–19 (part 1 of 2):

There is a difference of opinion about Luqman: is he a non-Arab (ʿajamī) or an Arab? He is said to be derived from al-luqam (mouthfuls). Whoever says he is a non-Arab prohibits his name from taking tanwin because of its being a proper name (ta'rif) and foreignness (ʿujma), and whoever says he is an Arab prohibits it from taking tanwin because of its being a proper name and the added alif and nun.

They also differed over whether he was a prophet (nabi) or a righteous man (rajul ṣāliḥ). The majority of scholars hold that he was not a prophet.

al-Wahidi transmitted from ʿIkrima, al-Suddi and al-Shaʿbi that he was a prophet, but the first view is more likely, for reasons that will come at the end of this discussion.

It is said that only ʿIkrima affirmed his prophethood, and the narrator of this from him is Jabir al-Ju'fi, who is extremely weak. He was Luqman ibn Baʿura ibn Nahur ibn Tarikh, and he was Azar, the father of Ibrahim. It is also said that he was Luqman ibn ʿAnqa ibn Marwan, a Nubian from the people of Ayla, mentioned by al-Suhayli.

Wahb said: he was the son of Ayyub's sister.

Muqatil said: he was the son of Ayyub's maternal aunt. He lived a thousand years, took knowledge from him, and used to give legal rulings (yufti) before the mission of Dawud. When Dawud was sent, he ceased giving rulings. It was said to him, "Why?" He said, "Shall I not be content, since I have been relieved of it?"

al-Waqidi said: he was a judge among the Children of Israel. The wisdom (hikma) that Allah gave him is understanding (fiqh), intellect, and correctness in speech. Whoever holds that he was a prophet explains the wisdom as prophethood. In ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي﴾ ("that give thanks to Me"), the *an* is explanatory (mufassira), because the granting of wisdom carries the meaning of saying.

It is also said that the implied sense is: "We said to him, give thanks to Me."

al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom, saying: give thanks to Me."

It is also said: "that give thanks to Me," so he gave thanks, and so he was wise through his thankfulness. Thanks to Allah is praise of Him in return for a blessing and obedience to what He has commanded.

Then Allah – glorified be He – made clear that thanks benefits no one but the one who gives thanks, so He said: ﴿ومَن يَشْكُرْ فَإنَّما يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ﴾ ("Whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own self"), because the benefit of that returns to him, and its fruit accrues to him, for by it blessings are preserved and by its means more of them are drawn from Allah – glorified be He. (p-1142) ﴿ومَن كَفَرَ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ غَنِيٌّ حَمِيدٌ﴾ ("And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy"), meaning: whoever makes the denial of blessings in place of thanking for them – Allah is Free of need from his thanks, not in need of it, Praiseworthy, deserving of praise from His creation for His favours upon them, blessings whose measure cannot be encompassed and whose number cannot be counted, even if none of His creatures praises Him, for every existing thing is speaking His praise with the tongue of its state.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: "Free of need from His creation, Praiseworthy in His acts."

﴿وإذْ قالَ لُقْمانُ لِابْنِهِ﴾ ("And when Luqman said to his son"). al-Suhayli said: the name of his son is Tharan according to Ibn Jarir and al-Qutaybi. al-Kalbi said: Mishkam. al-Naqqash said: Anʿam. It was said: Matan. al-Qushayri said: his son and his wife were disbelievers, and he never ceased admonishing them until they both embraced Islam. This sentence is coordinated with what preceded, and the implied sense is: "We gave Luqman wisdom when We made him grateful in himself, and when We made him an admonisher to others."

al-Zajjaj said: *idh* is in the accusative position governed by *ataynā*, and the meaning is: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom when he said..."

al-Nahhas said: I think this is an error, because there is a waw in the sentence and it prevents that.

The meaning of ﴿وهُوَ يَعِظُهُ﴾ ("while he was admonishing him") is that he addressed him with admonitions that encourage him toward monotheism and turn him away from polytheism. ﴿يابُنَيَّ لا تُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ﴾ ("O my son, do not associate anything with Allah"). The majority read *yā-bunayya* with a kasra on the ya. Ibn Kathir read it with sukun. Hafs read it with fatha. His prohibition of polytheism shows that he was a disbeliever, as mentioned earlier. The sentence ﴿إنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong") is a reason for what precedes. He began his admonition with forbidding polytheism because it is more important than anything else.

There is a difference about this sentence: it is said to be part of Luqman's speech, and it is said to be part of Allah's speech, in which case it is disconnected from what precedes. This is supported by the authentic hadith that when ﴿ولَمْ يَلْبِسُوا إيمانَهم بِظُلْمٍ﴾ ("and they have not mixed their belief with wrongdoing") [al-Anʿam: 82] was revealed, it was hard on the Companions, and they said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" So Allah revealed ﴿إنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾, and their hearts were content.

﴿ووَصَّيْنا الإنْسانَ بِوالِدَيْهِ﴾ ("And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents"). This injunction concerning the parents, and what follows up to His words ﴿بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("of what you used to do"), is an interjection between Luqman's speech, intended to emphasise what preceded of the prohibition of associating anything with Allah. The explanation of the injunction is His words ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِي ولِوالِدَيْكَ﴾ ("give thanks to Me and to your parents"), and what lies between them is an interjection between the explanation and the thing explained. Joining thanks to them with thanks to Allah indicates that their right is among the greatest rights upon the child, the greatest and the most binding. The meaning of ﴿حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ وهْنًا عَلى وهْنٍ﴾ ("his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness") is that she carried him in her womb while growing weaker each day upon weakness. It was also said: the meaning is that a woman is weak by nature, and then pregnancy weakens her further. *Wahnan* is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar).

al-Nahhas said: it is in the accusative as a second object, with the preposition removed, i.e., she carried him with weakness upon weakness. al-Zajjaj said the meaning is that carrying him necessitated that she weaken time after time. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of *ummuhu*, and ﴿عَلى وهْنٍ﴾ ("upon weakness") is a description of *wahnan*, i.e., a weakness existing upon weakness. The majority read the *hā'* with sukun in both places.

ʿĪsā al-Thaqafi – and it is a transmission from Abu ʿAmr – read it with fatha in both places, and both are dialectal forms. Qa'nab said:

*Is there for the blamers any forbidder who will restrain them? Indeed, in them are exhaustion and weakness.*

﴿وفِصالُهُ في عامَيْنِ﴾ ("and his weaning is in two years"). *al-Fisal* is weaning, which is that the child is separated from the mother. It is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the adverbial phrase.
