Al-Tabarani, Ibn Adi and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about God's words ﴿وَلَا تُصَعِّرْ خَدَّكَ لِلنَّاسِ﴾ (And do not turn your cheek away from people in contempt), and he said: "Twisting of the cheek (liyy al-shidq)." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning the same verse, that it means: do not be arrogant, so that you despise God's servants and turn away from them when they speak to you.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning the verse that it refers to the one who, when greeted, twists his neck like one who is arrogant.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 31, verses 20–28 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, finished with the story of Luqman, He returned to rebuking the polytheists, reproaching them and establishing the proofs against them. So He said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of their being subjected to the children of Adam is that they benefit from them. End of quote. So among the creatures of the heavens subjected to the children of Adam, meaning those from which they benefit, are the sun, the moon, the stars and the like.

Among that are the angels, for they are guardians of the children of Adam by the command of Allah, glory be to Him. Among the creatures of the earth subjected to the children of Adam are the stones, the soil, the crops, the trees, the fruit, the animals from which they benefit, the grass in which they pasture their animals, and other things too numerous to count. Thus the meaning of subjection (taskhir) is making the subjected thing such that the one for whom it is subjected benefits from it, whether it is obedient to him and under his control or not. ﴿And He has lavished upon you His favours, outward and inward﴾, meaning He has completed and perfected His favours upon you. It is said: "sabagha al-ni'mah" when the favour is complete and perfect.

The majority read "asbagha" with the sin. Ibn 'Abbas and Yahya ibn 'Umarah read "asba'a" (asbagha with the sad) in place of the sin.

"Ni'am" is the plural of "ni'mah" according to the reading of Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs. The rest read "ni'matan" with a sukun on the 'ayn, in the singular with tanwin, a collective noun (ism jins) used to mean the plural and to indicate abundance, as in His saying: ﴿And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. This is also the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

By the outward favours is meant what is perceived by the intellect or the senses and is known to whoever recognises it, and by the inward favours what is not perceived by people and is hidden from them.

It is said: the outward favours are health and completeness of form, and the inward are knowledge and intellect.

It is said: the outward favours are what is seen by the eyes, of wealth, standing, beauty and performing acts of obedience, and the inward are what a person finds within himself of knowledge of Allah and good certainty, and what Allah averts from him of calamities that are far off.

It is said: the outward favours are the blessings of this world, and the inward are the blessings of the Hereafter.

It is said: the outward favours are Islam and beauty, and the inward are what Allah has concealed from the servant of his bad deeds. ﴿Yet among mankind is he who disputes concerning Allah﴾, meaning concerning the affair of Allah, glory be to Him, regarding His oneness and His attributes, out of arrogance and obstinacy after the truth has become evident to him and the proof has been established against him. For this reason He said: ﴿without knowledge﴾, from intellect or transmission, ﴿nor guidance﴾ by which he might be guided to the path of rectitude, ﴿nor an illuminating Book﴾ revealed by Allah, glory be to Him. Rather it is mere obstinacy and pure contrariness. The tafsir of this verse has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down"﴾, meaning: when it is said to these disputers (the plural is according to the sense of "man"), "Follow what Allah has sent down through His Messenger of the Book," they cling to pure imitation, and ﴿they say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾, so that we worship what they used to worship of idols and walk the path they used to walk in their religion. Then He said, in the form of a question for censure and rebuke: ﴿Even though Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾, meaning: inviting their fathers whom they imitated in their religion, that is, they follow them in polytheism, and even if Satan was inviting them to what they were upon of polytheism. It is also permissible that it means he invites these followers to the punishment of the Blaze, because he adorned for them the following of their fathers and adhering to their religion. It is also permissible that it means he invites all the followers and the followed to the punishment: his invitation of the followed is by adorning polytheism for them, and his invitation of the followers is by adorning for them the religion of their fathers. The answer to "law" is omitted, meaning: he invites them and they follow them. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

How ugly is imitation, how great its harm to its possessor, how bad its outcome, and how evil its return upon the one who falls into it.

For the one who calls to it, instead of to what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger, is like one who wants to push away a moth from the flame of fire so that it will not burn; but it refuses that and falls headlong into the fire of the blaze and the punishment of the Blaze.

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾, meaning: entrusts his affair to Him, sincerely devotes his worship to Him and turns to Him wholeheartedly, ﴿while he is a doer of good﴾ in his deeds, because worship without excellence (ihsan) in it and without knowledge of what is required in it does not fall in the place where the worship of the doers of good falls.

It has been authentically reported from the Truthful and Confirmed One (ﷺ) that when Jibril asked him about ihsan, he said to him: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾, meaning he has held fast to the most reliable covenant and clung to it. This is a parable for the state of one who submits his face to Allah, likened to one who wants to ascend to the peak of a mountain and grasps the strongest loops of a rope hanging down from it. ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs﴾, meaning their final destination is to Him and not to anyone else.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Sulami and ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar read "wa man yuslim" with tashdid (yusallim). Al-Nahhas said: The takhfif (yuslim) in this is more well-known, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20].

﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you﴾, meaning: do not grieve over that, for his disbelief will not harm you. Having explained the state of the believers, He, glory be to Him, explained the state of the disbelievers, then threatened them with His saying: ﴿To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did﴾, meaning: We will tell them of the ugliness of their deeds and recompense them for them. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning: of what their breasts conceal; nothing of that is hidden from Him, so the secret is with Him like the open.

﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little﴾, meaning: We will keep them in this world for a brief period in which they enjoy themselves, for fleeting bliss is the least of little compared to lasting bliss.

The accusative of "qalilan" is because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an enjoyment that is little. ﴿Then We will force them to a harsh punishment﴾, meaning: We will compel them to the punishment of the Fire, for there is nothing heavier on the one who falls into it and is struck by it, and for this the word "ghilz" (harshness) is borrowed for it.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾, meaning: they acknowledge Allah as the Creator of that, because the matter is clear to them. This is an acknowledgement by them of what points to tawhid and the nullity of shirk, and for this He said: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾, meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Praise be to Allah" for your acknowledgement, so how do you worship other than Him and make others His partners? Or the meaning is: say "Praise be to Allah" for having guided us to His religion, and there is no praise for anyone else. Then He turned away from that and said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, meaning: they do not reflect or ponder until they know that the Creator of these things is the One who alone deserves worship besides Him.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ by ownership and creation, so none deserves worship but Him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ from others, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, meaning: the one deserving praise, or the one praised by His servants by tongue of speech or tongue of state.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, He followed it with what indicates that beyond that there is what no number encompasses and no limit confines. So He said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven seas after it, were ink﴾, meaning: if all the trees on the earth were pens. He used the singular "shajarah" because it is established in the science of meanings (ilm al-ma'ani) that the comprehensiveness of the singular noun is more inclusive, as though He said: every single tree, so that no single one of the kind of trees remains unless it has been made into pens. He used the plural "aqlam" for the purpose of multiplication, meaning: if each tree among the trees were counted as pens. Abu Hayyan said: This is from the placing of the singular in the place of the plural and the indefinite in the place of the definite, like His saying: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿and the sea, replenished by seven seas after it﴾, meaning: after it is exhausted, seven seas replenish it.

The majority read "wal-bahru" with raf', as a mubtada', with "yamudduhu" as its khabar, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while the encompassing sea, despite its vastness, is replenished by seven seas with a replenishment that does not cease. Thus Sibawayh said.

Al-Mubarrad said: the sea is in the nominative by a verb understood, its estimate being "and if the sea remained," with the clause "replenished by seven seas after it" as its circumstance. It was also said: it is in the nominative by coordination with the "anna" and what is in its scope.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wal-bahra" with nasb, coordinated with the noun of "anna," or by a hidden verb that it explains, "yamudduhu."

Ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan read "yumidduhu" with a damma on the present-tense letter and kasra on the mim, from amadda.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "wal-bahru midaduhu."

The answer to "law" is: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾, meaning: His words, which are an expression of His knowns.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: By the words, and Allah knows best, is meant what is in the decreed (al-maqdur) and not what has come out of it into existence. Al-Qaffal agreed with him, saying: the meaning is that if the trees were pens and the seas ink, and with them were written the wonders of Allah's creation which indicate His power and oneness, those wonders would not be exhausted.

Al-Qushayri said: al-Qaffal returned the meaning of "words" to the decreed things, but carrying the verse on the eternal speech (kalam qadim) is more preferable.

Al-Nahhas said: It has become clear that the "words" here are meant as knowledge and the realities of things, because He, mighty and majestic, knew before creating the creation what He would create in the heavens and the earth of anything, and knew what is in it of weights of atoms, and knew all the kinds and what is in them of a hair or limb, and what is in the tree of a leaf and what is in it of kinds of creation.

It was said: Quraysh said, "How much does Muhammad talk!" so this was revealed. This is narrated by al-Suddi. It was also said: when the verse "And you have not been given of knowledge except a little" [al-Isra: 85] was revealed concerning the Jews, they said, "How, when we have been given the Torah in which is the speech of Allah and His rulings?" so this was revealed.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: By "the sea" here is meant the sweet water that produces pens; as for salt water, it does not produce pens.

I say: how worthless this statement is and how little its benefit!

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾, meaning: Overpowering, nothing defeats Him, and no single one of His creatures departs from His wisdom and knowledge.

﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as that of a single soul﴾, meaning: only as the creation of a single soul and its resurrection.

Al-Nahhas said: So the grammarians estimated it as "like the creation of a soul," similar to His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, the power of Allah to resurrect all of creation and to create them is like His power to create one soul and resurrect one soul. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of everything that is heard, ﴿Seeing﴾ of everything that is seen.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from ʿAta', who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His saying: ﴿and He has lavished upon you His favours﴾ the verse. He said: This is from the treasures of my knowledge; I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it and he said: "As for the outward, it is what He made proportionate of your creation; as for the inward, it is what He concealed of your nakedness. Had He revealed it, your family would have spat on you, so what of others?"

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, al-Daylami and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His saying: ﴿and He has lavished upon you His favours, outward and inward﴾, and he said: 'As for the outward, it is Islam and what He made proportionate of your creation and what He lavished upon you of His provision; as for the inward, it is what concealed the evils of your deeds.'"

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, who said: The outward favour is Islam, and the inward favour is everything that conceals from you sins, faults and prescribed penalties.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him as well that he said regarding the interpretation of the verse: it is "There is no god but Allah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 31, verse 20–28 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him (Ibn Abbas) also, concerning His saying: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens and the sea [were ink]...﴾ the verse, that the rabbis of the Jews said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina: "O Muhammad, what do you say about your saying: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85]? Do you mean us, or your people?" He said: "Both." They said: "Do you not recite in what has come to you that we have been given the Torah, and in it is an explanation of everything?" He said: "Indeed, it is, in the knowledge of Allah, little." And Allah revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh related it from him with a longer version. Ibn Mardawayh also related from Ibn Mas'ud something similar.

It is said: "sabagha al-ni'mah" when the favour is complete and perfect.

It is said: the outward favours are what is seen by the eyes, of wealth, standing, beauty and performing acts of obedience, and the inward are what a person finds within himself of knowledge of Allah and good certainty, and what Allah averts from him of calamities that are far off.

It is said: the outward favours are the blessings of this world, and the inward are the blessings of the Hereafter.

Then He said, in the form of a question for censure and rebuke: ﴿Even though Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾, meaning: inviting their fathers whom they imitated in their religion, that is, they follow them in polytheism, and even if Satan was inviting them to what they were upon of polytheism. It is also permissible that it means he invites these followers to the punishment of the Blaze, because he adorned for them the following of their fathers and adhering to their religion. It is also permissible that it means he invites all the followers and the followed to the punishment: his invitation of the followed is by adorning polytheism for them, and his invitation of the followers is by adorning for them the religion of their fathers. The answer to "law" is omitted, meaning: he invites them and they follow them. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

How ugly is imitation, how great its harm to its possessor, how bad its outcome, and how evil its return upon the one who falls into it.

For the one who calls to it, instead of to what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger, is like one who wants to push away a moth from the flame of fire so that it will not burn; but it refuses that and falls headlong into the fire of the blaze and the punishment of the Blaze.

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾, meaning: entrusts his affair to Him, sincerely devotes his worship to Him and turns to Him wholeheartedly, ﴿while he is a doer of good﴾ in his deeds, because worship without excellence (ihsan) in it and without knowledge of what is required in it does not fall in the place where the worship of the doers of good falls.

It has been authentically reported from the Truthful and Confirmed One (ﷺ) that when Jibril asked him about ihsan, he said to him: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾, meaning he has held fast to the most reliable covenant and clung to it. This is a parable for the state of one who submits his face to Allah, likened to one who wants to ascend to the peak of a mountain and grasps the strongest loops of a rope hanging down from it. ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs﴾, meaning their final destination is to Him and not to anyone else.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Sulami and ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar read "wa man yuslim" with tashdid (yusallim). Al-Nahhas said: The takhfif (yuslim) in this is more well-known, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20].

Having explained the state of the believers, He, glory be to Him, explained the state of the disbelievers, then threatened them with His saying: ﴿To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did﴾, meaning: We will tell them of the ugliness of their deeds and recompense them for them. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning: of what their breasts conceal; nothing of that is hidden from Him, so the secret is with Him like the open.

The accusative of "qalilan" is because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an enjoyment that is little. ﴿Then We will force them to a harsh punishment﴾, meaning: We will compel them to the punishment of the Fire, for there is nothing heavier on the one who falls into it and is struck by it, and for this the word "ghilz" (harshness) is borrowed for it.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾, meaning: they acknowledge Allah as the Creator of that, because the matter is clear to them. This is an acknowledgement by them of what points to tawhid and the nullity of shirk, and for this He said: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾, meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Praise be to Allah" for your acknowledgement, so how do you worship other than Him and make others His partners? Or the meaning is: say "Praise be to Allah" for having guided us to His religion, and there is no praise for anyone else. Then He turned away from that and said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, meaning: they do not reflect or ponder until they know that the Creator of these things is the One who alone deserves worship besides Him.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ by ownership and creation, so none deserves worship but Him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ from others, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, meaning: the one deserving praise, or the one praised by His servants by tongue of speech or tongue of state.

So He said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven seas after it, were ink﴾, meaning: if all the trees on the earth were pens. He used the plural "aqlam" for the purpose of multiplication, meaning: if each tree among the trees were counted as pens. Ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan read "yumidduhu" with a damma on the present-tense letter and kasra on the mim, from amadda.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "wal-bahru midaduhu."

The answer to "law" is: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾, meaning: His words, which are an expression of His knowns.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: By "the sea" here is meant the sweet water that produces pens; as for salt water, it does not produce pens.

I say: how worthless this statement is and how little its benefit!

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾, meaning: Overpowering, nothing defeats Him, and no single one of His creatures departs from His wisdom and knowledge.

﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as that of a single soul﴾, meaning: only as the creation of a single soul and its resurrection.

It is said: "sabagha al-ni'mah" when the favour is complete and perfect.

It is said: the outward favours are health and completeness of form, and the inward are knowledge and intellect.

It is said: the outward favours are what is seen by the eyes, of wealth, standing, beauty and performing acts of obedience, and the inward are what a person finds within himself of knowledge of Allah and good certainty, and what Allah averts from him of calamities that are far off.

It is said: the outward favours are the blessings of this world, and the inward are the blessings of the Hereafter.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down"﴾, meaning: when it is said to these disputers (the plural is according to the sense of "man"), "Follow what Allah has sent down through His Messenger of the Book," they cling to pure imitation, and ﴿they say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾, so that we worship what they used to worship of idols and walk the path they used to walk in their religion. Then He said, in the form of a question for censure and rebuke: ﴿Even though Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾, meaning: inviting their fathers whom they imitated in their religion, that is, they follow them in polytheism, and even if Satan was inviting them to what they were upon of polytheism. It is also permissible that it means he invites these followers to the punishment of the Blaze, because he adorned for them the following of their fathers and adhering to their religion. It is also permissible that it means he invites all the followers and the followed to the punishment: his invitation of the followed is by adorning polytheism for them, and his invitation of the followers is by adorning for them the religion of their fathers. The answer to "law" is omitted, meaning: he invites them and they follow them. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

How ugly is imitation, how great its harm to its possessor, how bad its outcome, and how evil its return upon the one who falls into it.

For the one who calls to it, instead of to what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger, is like one who wants to push away a moth from the flame of fire so that it will not burn; but it refuses that and falls headlong into the fire of the blaze and the punishment of the Blaze.

﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little﴾, meaning: We will keep them in this world for a brief period in which they enjoy themselves, for fleeting bliss is the least of little compared to lasting bliss.

The accusative of "qalilan" is because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an enjoyment that is little. ﴿Then We will force them to a harsh punishment﴾, meaning: We will compel them to the punishment of the Fire, for there is nothing heavier on the one who falls into it and is struck by it, and for this the word "ghilz" (harshness) is borrowed for it.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾, meaning: they acknowledge Allah as the Creator of that, because the matter is clear to them. Then He turned away from that and said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, meaning: they do not reflect or ponder until they know that the Creator of these things is the One who alone deserves worship besides Him.

Ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan read "yumidduhu" with a damma on the present-tense letter and kasra on the mim, from amadda.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "wal-bahru midaduhu."

The answer to "law" is: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾, meaning: His words, which are an expression of His knowns.

It is said: "sabagha al-ni'mah" when the favour is complete and perfect.

"Ni'am" is the plural of "ni'mah" according to the reading of Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs. This is also the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

It is said: the outward favours are health and completeness of form, and the inward are knowledge and intellect.

It is said: the outward favours are what is seen by the eyes, of wealth, standing, beauty and performing acts of obedience, and the inward are what a person finds within himself of knowledge of Allah and good certainty, and what Allah averts from him of calamities that are far off.

It is said: the outward favours are the blessings of this world, and the inward are the blessings of the Hereafter.

It is said: the outward favours are Islam and beauty, and the inward are what Allah has concealed from the servant of his bad deeds. ﴿Yet among mankind is he who disputes concerning Allah﴾, meaning concerning the affair of Allah, glory be to Him, regarding His oneness and His attributes, out of arrogance and obstinacy after the truth has become evident to him and the proof has been established against him. For this reason He said: ﴿without knowledge﴾, from intellect or transmission, ﴿nor guidance﴾ by which he might be guided to the path of rectitude, ﴿nor an illuminating Book﴾ revealed by Allah, glory be to Him. Rather it is mere obstinacy and pure contrariness. The tafsir of this verse has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down"﴾, meaning: when it is said to these disputers (the plural is according to the sense of "man"), "Follow what Allah has sent down through His Messenger of the Book," they cling to pure imitation, and ﴿they say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾, so that we worship what they used to worship of idols and walk the path they used to walk in their religion. Then He said, in the form of a question for censure and rebuke: ﴿Even though Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾, meaning: inviting their fathers whom they imitated in their religion, that is, they follow them in polytheism, and even if Satan was inviting them to what they were upon of polytheism. It is also permissible that it means he invites these followers to the punishment of the Blaze, because he adorned for them the following of their fathers and adhering to their religion. It is also permissible that it means he invites all the followers and the followed to the punishment: his invitation of the followed is by adorning polytheism for them, and his invitation of the followers is by adorning for them the religion of their fathers. The answer to "law" is omitted, meaning: he invites them and they follow them. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

How ugly is imitation, how great its harm to its possessor, how bad its outcome, and how evil its return upon the one who falls into it.

For the one who calls to it, instead of to what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger, is like one who wants to push away a moth from the flame of fire so that it will not burn; but it refuses that and falls headlong into the fire of the blaze and the punishment of the Blaze.

The accusative of "qalilan" is because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an enjoyment that is little. ﴿Then We will force them to a harsh punishment﴾, meaning: We will compel them to the punishment of the Fire, for there is nothing heavier on the one who falls into it and is struck by it, and for this the word "ghilz" (harshness) is borrowed for it.

Then He turned away from that and said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, meaning: they do not reflect or ponder until they know that the Creator of these things is the One who alone deserves worship besides Him.

Ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan read "yumidduhu" with a damma on the present-tense letter and kasra on the mim, from amadda.

The answer to "law" is: ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾, meaning: His words, which are an expression of His knowns.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: By the words, and Allah knows best, is meant what is in the decreed (al-maqdur) and not what has come out of it into existence. Al-Qaffal agreed with him, saying: the meaning is that if the trees were pens and the seas ink, and with them were written the wonders of Allah's creation which indicate His power and oneness, those wonders would not be exhausted.

Al-Qushayri said: al-Qaffal returned the meaning of "words" to the decreed things, but carrying the verse on the eternal speech (kalam qadim) is more preferable.

Al-Nahhas said: It has become clear that the "words" here are meant as knowledge and the realities of things, because He, mighty and majestic, knew before creating the creation what He would create in the heavens and the earth of anything, and knew what is in it of weights of atoms, and knew all the kinds and what is in them of a hair or limb, and what is in the tree of a leaf and what is in it of kinds of creation.

It was said: Quraysh said, "How much does Muhammad talk!" so this was revealed. This is narrated by al-Suddi. It was also said: when the verse "And you have not been given of knowledge except a little" [al-Isra: 85] was revealed concerning the Jews, they said, "How, when we have been given the Torah in which is the speech of Allah and His rulings?" so this was revealed.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: By "the sea" here is meant the sweet water that produces pens; as for salt water, it does not produce pens.

I say: how worthless this statement is and how little its benefit!

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾, meaning: Overpowering, nothing defeats Him, and no single one of His creatures departs from His wisdom and knowledge.

﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as that of a single soul﴾, meaning: only as the creation of a single soul and its resurrection.

Al-Nahhas said: So the grammarians estimated it as "like the creation of a soul," similar to His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, the power of Allah to resurrect all of creation and to create them is like His power to create one soul and resurrect one soul. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of everything that is heard, ﴿Seeing﴾ of everything that is seen.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from ʿAta', who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about His saying: ﴿and He has lavished upon you His favours﴾ the verse. He said: This is from the treasures of my knowledge; I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it and he said: "As for the outward, it is what He made proportionate of your creation; as for the inward, it is what He concealed of your nakedness. Had He revealed it, your family would have spat on you, so what of others?"

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, al-Daylami and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His saying: ﴿and He has lavished upon you His favours, outward and inward﴾, and he said: 'As for the outward, it is Islam and what He made proportionate of your creation and what He lavished upon you of His provision; as for the inward, it is what concealed the evils of your deeds.'"

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, who said: The outward favour is Islam, and the inward favour is everything that conceals from you sins, faults and prescribed penalties.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him as well that he said regarding the interpretation of the verse: it is "There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him (Ibn Abbas) also, concerning His saying: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens and the sea [were ink]...﴾ the verse, that the rabbis of the Jews said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina: "O Muhammad, what do you say about your saying: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85]? Do you mean us, or your people?" He said: "Both." They said: "Do you not recite in what has come to you that we have been given the Torah, and in it is an explanation of everything?" He said: "Indeed, it is, in the knowledge of Allah, little." And Allah revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh related it from him with a longer version. Ibn Mardawayh also related from Ibn Mas'ud something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 31, verses 20–28 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, finished with the story of Luqman, He returned to rebuking the polytheists, reproaching them and establishing the proofs against them. So He said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of their being subjected to the children of Adam is that they benefit from them. End of quote. So among the creatures of the heavens subjected to the children of Adam, meaning those from which they benefit, are the sun, the moon, the stars and the like.

Among that are the angels, for they are guardians of the children of Adam by the command of Allah, glory be to Him. Among the creatures of the earth subjected to the children of Adam are the stones, the soil, the crops, the trees, the fruit, the animals from which they benefit, the grass in which they pasture their animals, and other things too numerous to count. Thus the meaning of subjection (taskhir) is making the subjected thing such that the one for whom it is subjected benefits from it, whether it is obedient to him and under his control or not. ﴿And He has lavished upon you His favours, outward and inward﴾, meaning He has completed and perfected His favours upon you. It is said: "sabagha al-ni'mah" when the favour is complete and perfect.

The majority read "asbagha" with the sin. Ibn 'Abbas and Yahya ibn 'Umarah read "asba'a" (asbagha with the sad) in place of the sin.

"Ni'am" is the plural of "ni'mah" according to the reading of Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs. The rest read "ni'matan" with a sukun on the 'ayn, in the singular with tanwin, a collective noun (ism jins) used to mean the plural and to indicate abundance, as in His saying: ﴿And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. This is also the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

By the outward favours is meant what is perceived by the intellect or the senses and is known to whoever recognises it, and by the inward favours what is not perceived by people and is hidden from them.

It is said: the outward favours are health and completeness of form, and the inward are knowledge and intellect.

It is said: the outward favours are what is seen by the eyes, of wealth, standing, beauty and performing acts of obedience, and the inward are what a person finds within himself of knowledge of Allah and good certainty, and what Allah averts from him of calamities that are far off.

It is said: the outward favours are the blessings of this world, and the inward are the blessings of the Hereafter.

It is said: the outward favours are Islam and beauty, and the inward are what Allah has concealed from the servant of his bad deeds. ﴿Yet among mankind is he who disputes concerning Allah﴾, meaning concerning the affair of Allah, glory be to Him, regarding His oneness and His attributes, out of arrogance and obstinacy after the truth has become evident to him and the proof has been established against him. For this reason He said: ﴿without knowledge﴾, from intellect or transmission, ﴿nor guidance﴾ by which he might be guided to the path of rectitude, ﴿nor an illuminating Book﴾ revealed by Allah, glory be to Him. Rather it is mere obstinacy and pure contrariness. The tafsir of this verse has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down"﴾, meaning: when it is said to these disputers (the plural is according to the sense of "man"), "Follow what Allah has sent down through His Messenger of the Book," they cling to pure imitation, and ﴿they say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾, so that we worship what they used to worship of idols and walk the path they used to walk in their religion. Then He said, in the form of a question for censure and rebuke: ﴿Even though Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾, meaning: inviting their fathers whom they imitated in their religion, that is, they follow them in polytheism, and even if Satan was inviting them to what they were upon of polytheism. It is also permissible that it means he invites these followers to the punishment of the Blaze, because he adorned for them the following of their fathers and adhering to their religion. It is also permissible that it means he invites all the followers and the followed to the punishment: his invitation of the followed is by adorning polytheism for them, and his invitation of the followers is by adorning for them the religion of their fathers. The answer to "law" is omitted, meaning: he invites them and they follow them. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

How ugly is imitation, how great its harm to its possessor, how bad its outcome, and how evil its return upon the one who falls into it.

For the one who calls to it, instead of to what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger, is like one who wants to push away a moth from the flame of fire so that it will not burn; but it refuses that and falls headlong into the fire of the blaze and the punishment of the Blaze.

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾, meaning: entrusts his affair to Him, sincerely devotes his worship to Him and turns to Him wholeheartedly, ﴿while he is a doer of good﴾ in his deeds, because worship without excellence (ihsan) in it and without knowledge of what is required in it does not fall in the place where the worship of the doers of good falls.

It has been authentically reported from the Truthful and Confirmed One (ﷺ) that when Jibril asked him about ihsan, he said to him: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾, meaning he has held fast to the most reliable covenant and clung to it. This is a parable for the state of one who submits his face to Allah, likened to one who wants to ascend to the peak of a mountain and grasps the strongest loops of a rope hanging down from it. ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs﴾, meaning their final destination is to Him and not to anyone else.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Sulami and ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar read "wa man yuslim" with tashdid (yusallim). Al-Nahhas said: The takhfif (yuslim) in this is more well-known, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20].

﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you﴾, meaning: do not grieve over that, for his disbelief will not harm you. Having explained the state of the believers, He, glory be to Him, explained the state of the disbelievers, then threatened them with His saying: ﴿To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did﴾, meaning: We will tell them of the ugliness of their deeds and recompense them for them. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning: of what their breasts conceal; nothing of that is hidden from Him, so the secret is with Him like the open.

﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little﴾, meaning: We will keep them in this world for a brief period in which they enjoy themselves, for fleeting bliss is the least of little compared to lasting bliss.

The accusative of "qalilan" is because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an enjoyment that is little. ﴿Then We will force them to a harsh punishment﴾, meaning: We will compel them to the punishment of the Fire, for there is nothing heavier on the one who falls into it and is struck by it, and for this the word "ghilz" (harshness) is borrowed for it.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾, meaning: they acknowledge Allah as the Creator of that, because the matter is clear to them. This is an acknowledgement by them of what points to tawhid and the nullity of shirk, and for this He said: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah"﴾, meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Praise be to Allah" for your acknowledgement, so how do you worship other than Him and make others His partners? Or the meaning is: say "Praise be to Allah" for having guided us to His religion, and there is no praise for anyone else. Then He turned away from that and said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, meaning: they do not reflect or ponder until they know that the Creator of these things is the One who alone deserves worship besides Him.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ by ownership and creation, so none deserves worship but Him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ from others, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, meaning: the one deserving praise, or the one praised by His servants by tongue of speech or tongue of state.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, He followed it with what indicates that beyond that there is what no number encompasses and no limit confines. So He said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven seas after it, were ink﴾, meaning: if all the trees on the earth were pens. He used the singular "shajarah" because it is established in the science of meanings (ilm al-ma'ani) that the comprehensiveness of the singular noun is more inclusive, as though He said: every single tree, so that no single one of the kind of trees remains unless it has been made into pens. He used the plural "aqlam" for the purpose of multiplication, meaning: if each tree among the trees were counted as pens. Abu Hayyan said: This is from the placing of the singular in the place of the plural and the indefinite in the place of the definite, like His saying: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿and the sea, replenished by seven seas after it﴾, meaning: after it is exhausted, seven seas replenish it.

The majority read "wal-bahru" with raf', as a mubtada', with "yamudduhu" as its khabar, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while the encompassing sea, despite its vastness, is replenished by seven seas with a replenishment that does not cease. Thus Sibawayh said.

Al-Mubarrad said: the sea is in the nominative by a verb understood, its estimate being "and if the sea remained," with the clause "replenished by seven seas after it" as its circumstance. It was also said: it is in the nominative by coordination with the "anna" and what is in its scope.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wal-bahra" with nasb, coordinated with the noun of "anna," or by a hidden verb that it explains, "yamudduhu."

Ibn Hurmuz and al-Hasan read "yumidduhu" with a damma on the present-tense letter and kasra on the mim, from amadda.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "wal-bahru midaduhu."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 31, verses 29–34:

The address in His words ﴿Do you not see﴾ is to everyone who is fit to receive it, or to the Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿That God causes the night to enter the day and causes the day to enter the night﴾ means that He makes each of them enter into the other. Its explanation has already been given in Surah al-Hajj and Surah al-An'am. ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ means that He made them submissive and compliant, rising and setting, as a determination of the appointed terms and a completion of benefits. The clause is coordinated with what precedes it, although the two differ. ﴿Each runs to a specified term﴾. Scholars have differed over what the specified term is. It was said to be the Day of Resurrection, and it was said to be the time of rising and the time of setting. The first view is preferable. The clause ﴿and that God is All-Aware of what you do﴾ is coordinated with ﴿that God causes the night to enter﴾, meaning: He is All-Aware of the deeds you do, none of which is hidden from Him, because whoever has power over such great matters, his power to know what you do is all the more certain.

The readers (*qurra'*) of the majority read ﴿what you do﴾ with the second-person form (تَعْمَلُونَ). As-Sulami, Nasr ibn 'Asim and ad-Duri from Abu 'Amr read it with the third-person form (يَعْمَلُونَ), as a report.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That﴾ refers to what has already been mentioned. The *ba'* in ﴿because God﴾ (بِأنَّ اللَّهَ) indicates cause, meaning: that is because of the fact that He, glorified be He, ﴿is the Truth﴾, while all else is falsehood. Alternatively, it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: He did that so that they would know that He is the Truth. ﴿And that what they call upon besides Him is falsehood﴾. Mujahid said: what they call upon besides Him is Satan. It was said to be what they associated with Him, whether an idol or something else, and this is preferable. ﴿And that God is the Most High, the Great﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿because God is the Truth﴾. The meaning is: that wondrous creation which He described in the preceding verses is an argument for God's truth, the falsity of everything else, and His exaltation and greatness. He is the Most High in His station, and possessor of greatness in His lordship and sovereignty.

Then He mentioned another kind of His marvellous creation and wondrous power, saying: ﴿Do you not see that the ships sail upon the sea by the favour of God﴾, meaning: by His kindness to you and His mercy towards you. This is among the greatest of His blessings upon you, because it saves you from drowning when you travel on the sea in search of provision. Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿the favours of God﴾ (بِنِعَماتِ اللَّهِ) as a plural of *ni'mah*. ﴿That He may show you some of His signs﴾. The *min* (مِن) here is partitive, meaning: that He may show you some of His signs.

Yahya ibn Salam said: this is the sailing of ships on the sea by the wind.

Ibn Shajarah said: what is meant by His words ﴿some of His signs﴾ is what they witness of God's power. An-Naqqash said: it is what God provides for them in the sea.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for everyone patient and grateful﴾. This clause gives the reason for what precedes it, meaning: indeed in what has been mentioned are great signs for everyone who has profound patience and abundant gratitude, who restrains himself from the disobedience of God and gives thanks for His blessings.

﴿And when a wave covers them like shadows﴾. He likened the wave, because of its size, to what shades a person, such as a mountain, a cloud, or something else. Although the wave is singular, it was likened to *zulal*, which is plural. The reason is that death comes one thing after another, and some of it is piled upon other parts of it. It was also said that *mawj* carries the sense of a plural, because it is a verbal noun. The root of *mawj* is movement and crowding, and from it one says *maja al-bahr* (the sea surged) and *maja an-nas* (the people surged). Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah read ﴿like shadows﴾ (كالظِّلالِ) as the plural of *zill*.

﴿They call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾, meaning: they call upon God alone, not relying on anyone else for their deliverance, because they know that none other can harm or benefit. However, customs and the imitation of the dead dominate their natures. When they fall into such a situation, they acknowledge God's oneness and make their religion sincerely His, seeking deliverance and safety from what they have fallen into.

﴿But when He brings them safe to land﴾, they divide into two groups. One group is ﴿moderate﴾ (مُقْتَصِدٌ), meaning: one who fulfils what he pledged to God at sea, namely sincerity of religion to Him, and remains upon that after God has delivered him from the terror of the sea and brought him safely out to land.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of *muqtasid* is a believer who holds fast to monotheism and obedience. Mujahid said: *muqtasid* means one who is moderate in speech while concealing disbelief. The first view is preferable. In the passage there is an omission, and the sense is: ﴿so among them is a moderate one, and among them is a disbeliever﴾. His words ﴿None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾ indicate this omitted part. *Khatr* is the worst and most shameful treachery. From it comes the verse of al-A'sha:

*With al-Ablaq al-Fard of Taymaa is his dwelling, a fortress impregnable, and a neighbour who is no betrayer.*

Al-Jawhari said: *al-khatr* is treachery. One says *khatarahu*, so he is a *khattar* (a treacherous one). Al-Mawardi said: this is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it means the denier. The denial of signs is rejecting them, and *kafur* means one who is greatly ungrateful for the blessings of God, glorified be He.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no parent will avail for a child﴾, meaning: no parent will benefit his child in anything, nor will he profit him in any way of benefit, because he is preoccupied with himself. Its explanation has already been given in Surah al-Baqarah. ﴿Nor will a child avail at all for his parent﴾. He, glorified be He, mentioned two kinds of kin, namely the parent and the child, who are the utmost in tenderness and compassion towards one another. Other kin are then all the less likely to avail, let alone strangers. O God, make us among those who hope for none but You and rely on none but You.

﴿Indeed God's promise is true﴾. It does not fail. What He has promised of good and what He has threatened of evil will certainly come to pass. ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾ with its adornments, for it is passing and departing. ﴿Nor let the Deceiver deceive you about God﴾.

The majority read ﴿the Deceiver﴾ (الغَرُورِ) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Gharur is Satan, because it is his nature to deceive creation, to beguile them with false wishes, to distract them from the Hereafter, and to turn them away from the path of truth.

Simak ibn Harb, Abu Haywah and Ibn as-Sumayfa' read it with a damma on the ghayn (الغُرُورِ), as the verbal noun of *gharra yaghurru ghuruṙan*. It may also be a verbal noun used as an adjective for Satan, for emphasis.

﴿Indeed God has knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning: knowledge of the time at which it will occur.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning of this statement is negation, that is, none knows it except God, mighty and majestic.

An-Nahhas said: the sense of negation arose from what was reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His words ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ (al-An'am 59), that these are the five. ﴿He sends down the rain﴾ at the times He has determined for its descent, and none knows that but Him. ﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾, whether male or female, righteous or wicked. ﴿No soul knows﴾ of souls, whatever it may be, without distinction between angels, prophets, jinn and humans, ﴿what it will earn tomorrow﴾, whether earnings of religion or earnings of this world. ﴿No soul knows in what land it will die﴾, meaning: in what place God has decreed death for it.

The majority read ﴿and He sends down the rain﴾ (وَيُنَزِّلُ الغَيْثَ) with the doubled *zay* (مُشَدَّدًا). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a single *zay* (مُخَفَّفًا).

The majority read ﴿in what land﴾ (بِأيِّ أرْضٍ). Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Musa al-Ahwazi read *bi-ayyatin* (بِأيَّةِ). Al-Farra' permitted this, though it is a weak dialect. Al-Akhfash said: one may say *marartu bi-jariyatin ayyu jariyatin* (I passed by a girl, what a girl). Az-Zajjaj said: whoever claims that he knows anything of these five has disbelieved in the Qur'an, because he has contradicted it.
